solution:
\(B(6,8)\) and \(C(-8,6)\) both lie on \(x^2+y^2=100\), and \(A\) is only required to lie on the same circle.

So \(A\) can be any point of the circle other than \(B\) and \(C\). For example, both \((-6,8)\) and \((-6,-8)\) satisfy \(x^2+y^2=100\), so there are infinitely many positions for \(A\) and no single one is fixed by the data.

Hence (D).
note: BC has length sqrt200, not a diameter, so no right-angle argument applies; A is any other point of the circle. Key D right.

solution:
The latus rectum is vertical (\(x=-2\)), so the axis is horizontal.

The focus is at \((-2,0)\) (midpoint), and the latus rectum has length \(4a=8\), so \(a=2\).

The parabola can open left, with vertex \((0,0)\): \(y^2=-8x\), or open right, with vertex \((-4,0)\): \(y^2=8(x+4)\). So there are 2 parabolas.

Hence (B).
note: Latus rectum 8 = 4a gives a=2, focus (-2,0); left-opening is y^2=-8x, right-opening y^2=8(x+4). Count 2 stands.

solution:
\(y^2-kx+8=0\Rightarrow y^2=k\left(x-\tfrac{8}{k}\right)\), so the vertex is at \(x=\tfrac{8}{k}\) and \(4A=k\).

The directrix is \(x=\tfrac{8}{k}-\tfrac{k}{4}=1\Rightarrow k^2+4k-32=0\Rightarrow k=4\) or \(k=-8\).

Only \(k=4\) appears among the options.

Hence (C).
note: k^2+4k-32=0 has roots 4 and -8; the solution drops -8 silently. Only k=4 is among the options.

solution:
\(2x^2 + 3y^2 = 1\) gives \(\dfrac{x^2}{1/2} + \dfrac{y^2}{1/3} = 1\), so \(a^2 = 1/2\), \(b^2 = 1/3\).

Tangent \(y = x + \lambda\) has \(m = 1\); the condition \(\lambda^2 = a^2 m^2 + b^2 = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6\) gives \(\lambda = \pm\sqrt{5/6}\).

Only \(\sqrt{5/6}\) is among the options.

Hence (C).
note: lambda^2 = 5/6 gives lambda = +/- sqrt(5/6); only the positive value is an option.

solution:
The given equation can be rewritten as

\((y - 1)^{2} = 2(x - 2)\)

or \(Y^{2} = 4AX\), where \(Y = y - 1\), \(X = x - 2\), \(4A = 2\).

The directrix is \(X = -A \Rightarrow x - 2 = -\tfrac{1}{2}\), so \(x = \tfrac{3}{2}\).

Hence (B).
note: Rewriting gives (y-1)^2=2(x-2), directrix x=3/2, key B right; trailing text is another question's working.

solution:
It represents a hyperbola if the equation is in the form \(\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} - \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1\).

So \(12 - k > 0 \Rightarrow k < 12\), and \(8 - k < 0 \Rightarrow k > 8\).

On combining both, we get \(8 < k < 12\). (For \(k < 8\) both denominators are positive, which is an ellipse.)

Therefore it represents a hyperbola if \(8 < k < 12\).

Hence (C).
note: Hyperbola needs 12-k>0 and 8-k<0, i.e. k<12 and k>8, so 8<k<12; the solution wrongly writes 8-k<0 as k<8.

solution:
Roots of \(x^2-x+1=0\) are \(\alpha=e^{i\pi/3},\beta=e^{-i\pi/3}\).

Then \(\alpha^{100}=e^{i100\pi/3}\) and \(\beta^{100}=e^{-i100\pi/3}\); \(100\pi/3 \equiv 4\pi/3 \pmod{2\pi}\).

So \(\alpha^{100}+\beta^{100}=2\cos(4\pi/3)=-1\) and \(\alpha^{100}-\beta^{100}=2i\sin(4\pi/3)=-i\sqrt{3}\).

The ratio \(\left|\frac{-1}{-i\sqrt{3}}\right|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\). Hence (D).
note: Roots of x^2-x+1 are e^{±i pi/3}, not -omega; the rest holds.

solution:
We have \(\frac{1-i}{1+i}=\frac{(1-i)^2}{(1+i)(1-i)}=\frac{1-2i+i^2}{1-i^2}=\frac{-2i}{2}=-i\).

So \(\left(\frac{1-i}{1+i}\right)^n=(-i)^n\), which is purely imaginary when \(n\) is odd.

For \(n=1\): \((-i)^1=-i\), negative imaginary part.

For \(n=3\): \((-i)^3=i\), positive imaginary part. Hence \(n=3\), (B).

\(z^{\frac13}=p+iq\Rightarrow z=(p+iq)^3=p^3+3p^2(iq)+3p(iq)^2+(iq)^3\)

\(\Rightarrow x-iy=p^{3}-3pq^{2}+i\left(3p^{2}q-q^{3}\right)\)

\(\therefore x=p^{3}-3pq^{2}\Rightarrow\frac{x}{p}=p^{2}-3q^{2}\)

\(y=q^{3}-3p^{2}q\Rightarrow\frac{y}{q}=q^{2}-3p^{2}\)

\(\therefore\frac{x}{p}+\frac{y}{q}=-2p^{2}-2q^{2}\), so the required value is \(-2\). Hence (A).
note: (p+iq)^3 = p^3+3p^2(iq)+3p(iq)^2+(iq)^3; the stated expansion is false.

solution:
\(a=e^{i\alpha},\ b=e^{i\beta},\ c=\cos\gamma+i\sin\gamma=e^{i\gamma}\).

Then \(\frac bc+\frac ca+\frac ab=e^{i(\beta-\gamma)}+e^{i(\gamma-\alpha)}+e^{i(\alpha-\beta)}=1\).

The imaginary part of the left side is \(\sin(\beta-\gamma)+\sin(\gamma-\alpha)+\sin(\alpha-\beta)\), and the right side is real, so this equals \(0\).

Hence \(\sin(\alpha-\beta)+\sin(\beta-\gamma)+\sin(\gamma-\alpha)=0\), (A).
note: b/c=e^{i(beta-gamma)}, c/a=e^{i(gamma-alpha)}, a/b=e^{i(alpha-beta)}; imaginary part gives the sum 0.

solution:
Cube root of unity \(=-\frac12\left(1+i\sqrt3\right)\), so A matches 4.

A square root of \(-1\) is \(i\), so B matches 3.

\((1-i)^3=1-3i+3i^2-i^3=1-3i-3+i=-2-2i=-2(1+i)\), so C matches 1.

\((1+i)^2=1+2i+i^2=2i\), so D matches 2. Hence (C).
note: (1-i)^3 = 1-3i+3i^2-i^3 = -2-2i; the written expansion is false though result is right.

solution:
Given \(|z+\omega|=|z-\omega|\)

\(\Rightarrow|z+\omega|^{2}=|z-\omega|^{2}\)

\(\Rightarrow(z+\omega)\left(\overline{z+\omega}\right)=(z-\omega)\left(\overline{z-\omega}\right)\)

\(\Rightarrow z\overline{z}+z\overline{\omega}+\overline{z}\omega+\omega\overline{\omega}=z\overline{z}-z\overline{\omega}-\omega\overline{z}+\omega\overline{\omega}\)

\(\Rightarrow z\overline{\omega}+\omega\overline{z}=0\)

Since \(\omega\overline{z}=\overline{z\overline{\omega}}\), this says \(2\,\mathrm{Re}(z\overline{\omega})=0\), so \(z\overline{\omega}\) is purely imaginary (zero allowed). Hence (D).
note: Expanding gives z*conj(w)+w*conj(z)=2Re(z conj w)=0, i.e. z conj(w) purely imaginary, not z=0 or w=0.

solution:
\(\left|z+\frac12\right|\ge\big||z|-\frac12\big|=|z|-\frac12\ge2-\frac12=\frac32\), with equality at \(z=-2\).

There is no upper bound, but the minimum value is \(\frac32\).

Since \(1<\frac32<2\), the minimum lies in the interval \((1,2)\). Hence (D).
note: |z|>=2 gives |z+1/2| >= |z|-1/2 >= 3/2, attained at z=-2; no upper bound. Minimum 3/2 lies in (1,2).

solution:
\(1+\sqrt3 i=2\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i\right)=2e^{i\pi/3}\)

So \((1+\sqrt3 i)^{n/2}=2^{n/2}e^{in\pi/6}\).

This is positive real exactly when \(\frac{n\pi}{6}=2k\pi\), i.e. \(n=12k\). (For \(n=6\) it equals \(-8\), negative.)

The smallest positive value is \(n=12\). Hence (C).
note: 1+sqrt3 i = 2e^{i pi/3}; power is 2^{n/2}e^{i n pi/6}, positive real only for n=12k. n=6 gives -8.

solution:
\(\frac32+i\frac{\sqrt3}2=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}(\sqrt3+i)=\sqrt3\left(\cos\frac\pi6+i\sin\frac\pi6\right)\)

So \(\left(\frac32+i\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)^{50}=3^{25}\left(\cos\frac{50\pi}6+i\sin\frac{50\pi}6\right)\).

\(\frac{50\pi}{6}=8\pi+\frac\pi3\), so \(x=\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12\) and \(y=\sin\frac\pi3=\frac{\sqrt3}2\).

The ordered pair is \(\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)\). Hence (D).
